*Manuscript submitted to Water Resources Research*

__Cybernetics of Hydro Systems: A Unified Control\-Theoretic Framework__

__for Water Network Operations__

__Xiaohui Lei__1\*

1 School of Water Resources, Hebei University of Engineering, Handan 056038, China

\*Corresponding author: Xiaohui Lei \(lxh@iwhr\.com\)

__Key Points:__

•  Water systems' unique operational singularity—five co\-occurring properties—demands a dedicated control science\.

•  A unified transfer function family subsumes all low\-order hydrodynamic models across water infrastructure subsectors\.

•  Multi\-Agent System architecture with five Water Systems Autonomy Levels charts a path to autonomous operation\.

__Abstract__

Water infrastructure operational intelligence remains decades behind automotive, aerospace, and power systems\. We propose Cybernetics of Hydro Systems \(CHS\) as a unified control\-theoretic framework addressing this gap\. CHS establishes an operational singularity thesis—five co\-occurring properties unique to water systems—and a structural isomorphism proposition demonstrating that all water subsectors share a common six\-element mathematical structure\. The mathematical backbone is a unified transfer function family proving that all low\-order hydrodynamic models—IDZ, Muskingum, Nash cascade, reservoir continuity, pipe compliance—are special cases of a single three\-parameter family within a five\-level model–control hierarchy\. Eight governing principles organized into dual tetrads guide systematic design\. A Multi\-Agent System architecture integrating Hierarchical Distributed Control, Operational Design Domain, and Cognitive Intelligence translates theory into practice, while five Water Systems Autonomy Levels chart the progression toward full autonomous operation\. Illustrative applications demonstrate cross\-sector transferability\.

__Plain Language Summary__

Humanity has built vast networks of canals, pipelines, and dams worth trillions of dollars\. But operating them—deciding when to open a gate or respond to a flood—still relies mostly on human experience\. Cars are learning to drive themselves, aircraft fly on autopilot, and power grids self\-balance, yet water systems lag far behind\. A key reason is that water failures are irreversible: you cannot un\-flood a city or un\-dry a river\. This makes it dangerous to simply copy automation approaches from other industries\. We propose a unifying theory called Cybernetics of Hydro Systems \(CHS\), showing that all water systems—whether irrigation canals, reservoirs, urban pipelines, or inter\-basin transfers—share the same mathematical control structure and can be understood through eight operating principles and a five\-level hierarchy of models\. Building on this theory, we introduce a Multi\-Agent System architecture that pairs physics\-based control \(for safety\) with AI reasoning \(for intelligence\), and define five Water Systems Autonomy Levels—a classification system analogous to self\-driving car levels—to chart the path from manual operation to autonomous control\. CHS provides a scientific foundation for safely and progressively automating water infrastructure\.

__Keywords: __water network control; autonomous operation; structural isomorphism; model predictive control; multi\-agent systems; operational design domain; water systems autonomy levels

__1  Introduction__

Water infrastructure constitutes one of the largest classes of engineered systems on Earth\. Globally, more than 500,000 km of inter\-basin and intra\-basin water conveyance channels are in operation, alongside millions of kilometers of pressurized urban distribution networks \(UNESCO, 2024\)\. The cumulative global investment is estimated at several trillion dollars\. Yet a striking asymmetry persists: the science of designing and constructing water infrastructure is mature, while the science of operating it in real time remains nascent\. A cross\-sector comparison \(Lei, 2025a\) found that operational autonomy of water conveyance systems worldwide remains at Level 0–Level 1—equivalent to manual driving with minimal assistance—while automotive has achieved Level 2–3 and commercial aviation operates at Level 4–5 in cruise phases\.

This gap is not merely technological—it is paradigmatic\. The automotive sector’s progression from cruise control to advanced driver\-assistance systems has been guided by coherent control theory and formalized through SAE J3016 autonomy levels \(SAE International, 2021\)\. Aerospace fly\-by\-wire systems are underpinned by decades of flight control science\. Power system operations rest on foundations laid by Kundur \(1994\), where automatic generation control maintains frequency stability across continental\-scale grids\. The water sector possesses no comparable unifying framework\. Canal automation \(Litrico & Fromion, 2009\), reservoir optimization \(Labadie, 2004\), urban pressure management \(Brdys & Ulanicki, 1994\), and hydropower scheduling \(Giuliani et al\., 2021\) have evolved as disconnected disciplinary silos, each developing bespoke solutions without a shared theoretical language\.

Why has the water sector lagged so persistently? We identify a structural reason deeper than institutional inertia, which we term the operational singularity thesis \(Section 2\)\. We also document a pervasive disciplinary fragmentation—different water communities independently naming and modeling mathematically equivalent control problems—that has impeded cross\-sector learning \(Section 2\.2\)\. Cybernetics of Hydro Systems \(CHS\) is proposed as the dedicated control science that addresses both challenges\. The term ‘cybernetics’ deliberately evokes Wiener’s \(1948\) original vision of a transdisciplinary science of communication and control—precisely the intellectual mission of CHS\.

The preliminary theoretical foundation was first proposed by the author in Chinese\-language publications: the principles of feedback and decoupling within a four\-element technical system \(Lei, 2025a\), autonomous water networks with multi\-level intelligence classification \(Lei, 2025b\), X\-in\-the\-Loop verification methodology \(Lei, 2025c\), and the pathway from static water balance to dynamic control \(Lei, 2025d\)\. The present paper substantially extends this prior work in seven directions: \(1\) formalizing the operational singularity thesis as a formal definition with five necessary conditions; \(2\) introducing the six\-element formalization with a structural isomorphism proposition across five subsectors; \(3\) establishing a five\-level model–control hierarchy with a model–layer correspondence theorem; \(4\) expanding from two to eight governing principles organized into dual tetrads with inter\-principle tradeoffs; \(5\) providing illustrative applications including multi\-pool distributed MPC and cross\-sector transfer across three subsectors; and \(6\) introducing the Multi\-Agent System \(MAS\) architecture and Water Systems Autonomy Levels \(WSAL\) as the implementation bridge from CHS theory to engineering practice\.

The paper is structured as follows\. Section 2 establishes the case for why water systems demand a dedicated control science, through the operational singularity thesis and evidence of disciplinary fragmentation\. Section 3 presents the CHS formalization: definitions, propositions, and the six\-element architecture\. Section 4 develops the model–control hierarchy—the mathematical backbone of CHS\. Section 5 articulates the eight governing principles\. Section 6 provides illustrative applications\. Section 7 translates CHS theory into an implementable architecture through the MAS framework and WSAL classification\. Section 8 positions CHS within the broader landscape\. Section 9 presents the research agenda and testable predictions\. Section 10 concludes\.

__2  Why Water Systems Demand a Dedicated Control Science__

Before presenting the CHS formalization, we establish two independent arguments for why water systems require a dedicated operational science rather than direct application of existing control frameworks from other infrastructure domains\.

__2\.1  The Operational Singularity: Five Defining Properties__

Water systems face a combination of properties that, taken together, is absent from any other major infrastructure domain\. We formalize this as the first defining concept of CHS\.

__*Definition 1 \(Operational Singularity\)\. *__A water conveyance or distribution system exhibits operational singularity if and only if it simultaneously possesses all five of the following properties:

__\(OS1\) Failure irreversibility\. __Consequences of constraint violation are physically irreversible within operational time horizons: a levee breach cannot be un\-flooded, an ecological flow violation that kills aquatic organisms cannot be undone, a contamination event that enters a distribution network cannot be recalled\.

__\(OS2\) Extreme spatial distribution\. __The system spans tens to thousands of kilometers, with transport delays of hours to days, creating spatially indexed control problems far exceeding the scale of a chemical plant or aircraft\.

__\(OS3\) Slow, physically distributed actuators\. __Gates, valves, and pumps respond in minutes, are located along the flow path rather than concentrated in a control room, and their number scales linearly with system length\.

__\(OS4\) Open\-boundary environmental coupling\. __Water systems are subject to weather, ecology, and geology in ways that enclosed industrial processes are not, making disturbance characterization fundamentally harder: the same canal faces ice formation in winter, algal blooms in summer, and flash floods in monsoon season\.

__\(OS5\) Impossibility of controlled failure testing\. __Unlike automotive crash tests, aerospace wind tunnels, or power system islanding experiments, one cannot deliberately flood a canal or breach a dam to calibrate controllers\. There is no ‘water tunnel’ analog to the wind tunnel\.

The operational singularity thesis asserts that it is the co\-occurrence of all five properties, not any single one, that defines the water control challenge\. Other infrastructure domains share individual properties—nuclear power plants face failure irreversibility \(OS1\), continental power grids have spatial distribution \(OS2\)—but no other major infrastructure domain routinely combines all five at the scales characteristic of water systems\. This co\-occurrence has three structural consequences\. First, it explains why the water sector has been conservative about automation: operators intuitively understand that the cost of control failure exceeds any efficiency gain, and there is no safe way to test near\-failure behavior\. Second, it explains why direct method transfer from other domains is insufficient: automotive and aerospace certification regimes \(SAE International, 2021; ISO, 2022; RTCA, 2011\) assume the availability of accelerated testing that water systems cannot provide\. Third, it establishes why a dedicated science is required—one that places constraint inviolability and provable safety at its theoretical center\.

__2\.2  Disciplinary Fragmentation: Different Names, Same Mathematics__

The second argument for a dedicated science is empirical: the water research community has organized itself by application domain rather than by operational science, leading to duplicated effort and missed cross\-sector learning\. Four largely non\-overlapping communities—canal automation, reservoir operations, urban water distribution, and watershed hydrology—have independently developed different terminologies, modeling conventions, and solution traditions for mathematically equivalent concepts\.

Table 1 presents a systematic mapping of seven fundamental control concepts across four water subsectors, with representative references for each domain’s terminology\. The mapping reveals that the governing dynamics in all subsectors are hyperbolic conservation laws—Saint\-Venant equations for open channels \(Litrico & Fromion, 2009\), water hammer equations for pressurized pipes \(Wylie & Streeter, 1993\), and Muskingum routing for watersheds \(Cunge, 1969\)—each simplified to low\-order transfer functions for control design\. The Integrator–Delay model used in canal control \(Schuurmans, 1997\) is mathematically isomorphic to the Nash cascade in watershed hydrology \(Nash, 1957\): in each case, an integrator represents storage capacity and a delay represents wave propagation—the same mathematical structure wearing different terminological clothing\.

The practical consequence of this fragmentation is measurable\. Castelletti et al\. \(2023\), in a ten\-author cross\-domain review of Model Predictive Control spanning reservoirs, open channels, and urban water networks, explicitly diagnosed that the related literature is scattered across heterogeneous applications with case\-specific formulations that are hardly transferable across systems\. Creaco et al\. \(2019\) noted that real\-time control has decades of implementation history in urban drainage but remains nascent in water distribution—two subsectors separated by organizational boundaries rather than technical ones\. The frequency\-domain controller design methods developed by Litrico and Fromion \(2004, 2009\) for canal pools have not been adapted for pressure controller design in distribution systems, where empirical tuning remains standard practice\. The stochastic dynamic programming methods refined over decades for reservoir optimization \(Stedinger et al\., 1984; Giuliani et al\., 2021\) have had negligible influence on long\-term scheduling of inter\-basin transfer systems, despite the evident mathematical parallels\.

__2\.3  The IWRM–Operations Gap__

The fragmentation documented above parallels a broader gap in the water governance discourse\. Integrated Water Resources Management \(IWRM\) has been the dominant paradigm for water sector coordination since the Dublin Principles \(1992\)\. Yet Biswas \(2004\) argued that IWRM’s definition remains amorphous and operationally unimplementable, with no activity worldwide scoring above 30 on a 1–100 integration scale\. This critique pinpoints a structural limitation: IWRM addresses integration at the governance and planning level—institutional coordination, stakeholder participation, policy harmonization—but provides no framework for operational integration at the control\-theoretic level\.

CHS fills this gap as the operational\-scientific complement to IWRM’s governance perspective\. Where IWRM asks ‘Which institutions should coordinate?’, CHS asks ‘What mathematical structure do their systems share, and how should controllers be designed to exploit that structure?’ Once the terminological mapping of Table 1 is recognized, a control engineer fluent in CHS can move between canal regulation, reservoir scheduling, and urban pressure management by re\-parameterizing the same algorithmic framework—achieving through unified operational science what institutional reform alone has not delivered\.

__3  The CHS Formalization__

Having established why a dedicated science is needed, we now present its formal structure\. CHS rests on three pillars: a formal definition of water control systems, a structural isomorphism proposition, and a six\-element architecture that instantiates the proposition across subsectors\.

__3\.1  Formal Definition of Water Control Systems__

__*Definition 2 \(Water Control System\)\. *__A water control system in the CHS sense is a six\-tuple Σ = \(P, A, S, D, C, O\) where P \(Plant\) is a dynamical system governed by hyperbolic conservation laws with state x ∈ X ⊆ ℝⁿ, A \(Actuator\) is the set of controllable boundary inputs u ∈ U\(x; θ\) ⊆ ℝᵐ, S \(Sensor\) is the observation map y = h\(x\) \+ v with measurement noise v, D \(Disturbance\) is the exogenous forcing d\(t\) entering through open boundaries, C \(Constraint\) is the set of hard inequality constraints g\(x, u; θ\) ≤ 0 whose violation is irreversible \(OS1\), and O \(Objective\) is the performance criterion J to be minimized subject to C\. The system exhibits operational singularity \(Definition 1\) and its dynamics satisfy five structural properties \(Proposition 1\)\.

This definition elevates Constraints and Objectives to first\-class elements alongside the traditional plant–actuator–sensor triple\. The elevation is not cosmetic: in most control engineering applications, constraints are soft penalties that can be temporarily violated at some cost; in water systems, constraint violation \(flooding, ecological destruction, contamination\) is irreversible per OS1\. This distinction is the formal expression of the operational singularity at the architectural level\.

__3\.2  Structural Isomorphism__

The foundational claim of CHS is not merely that water systems can be written in state\-space form—any physical system can\. Rather, we identify five specific structural properties shared across all water subsectors that collectively distinguish the water control problem from other infrastructure domains\.

__*Proposition 1 \(Structural Isomorphism\)\. *__All water conveyance and distribution systems, as defined in Definition 2, share the following five structural properties within a common controlled dynamical system representation:

__\(S1\) Hyperbolic conservation\-law dynamics: __dx/dt = f\(x, u, d; θ\), where f derives from the Saint\-Venant equations \(open channels\), the water hammer equations \(pressurized conduits\), or their approximations\. The hyperbolic character implies finite wave propagation speed and the possibility of shock formation\.

__\(S2\) Spatially distributed actuators: __u ∈ U\(x; θ\) ⊆ ℝᵐ, where actuators \(gates, valves, pumps\) are physically distributed along the flow path, their number m scaling with system length, and their feasible set U depends on system state x and physical parameters θ\.

__\(S3\) State\-dependent transport delays: __τᵈ\(x\), where wave propagation time depends on flow depth and velocity \(in open channels via celerity c = √\(gA/T\)\), creating delays that vary with operating conditions\.

__\(S4\) Hard safety constraints with irreversible violation: __g\(x, u; θ\) ≤ 0, where constraint violation triggers irreversible consequences \(OS1\)\. These are not soft penalties but absolute barriers in the optimization landscape\.

__\(S5\) Open\-boundary environmental coupling: __d\(t\) enters through spatially distributed open boundaries subject to weather, ecology, and geology \(OS4\), making complete stochastic characterization of disturbances infeasible\.

Properties S1–S3 establish the mathematical form; properties S4–S5 establish the operational context\. The structural isomorphism claim is that every water system in Definition 2 possesses all five properties, and that the specific instantiation of each property \(which PDE, which actuator type, which constraint\) varies across subsectors but the mathematical structure is invariant\. This invariance is what enables cross\-sector transfer of control methods \(Section 6\.3\)\.

__*Scope and limits\.*__ Proposition 1 applies to water conveyance and distribution systems with wave\-propagation physics and continuous operations—covering irrigation canals, hydropower cascades, urban distribution networks, navigation waterways, and inter\-basin transfers\. Two important subsectors fall outside this scope\. First, groundwater systems governed by Darcy's law exhibit fundamentally diffusive dynamics without wave propagation; S1 \(hyperbolic conservation\-law dynamics\) does not hold, and S3 \(state\-dependent transport delays\) manifests as diffusion timescales rather than wave delays\. Second, stormwater and combined sewer overflow \(CSO\) systems, while hydraulically governed by Saint\-Venant\-type equations, operate episodically rather than continuously, violating the sustained\-operation assumption implicit in S3 \(slow actuators\)\. This boundary is a feature, not a limitation: it sharpens the claim by specifying precisely which systems CHS unifies\. The covered systems represent the vast majority of water infrastructure by investment value and operational complexity\.

__3\.3  Six\-Element Architecture: Cross\-Sector Instantiation__

Table 2 demonstrates the six\-element structure \(Definition 2\) across five water subsectors\. Lei \(2025a\) first noted this isomorphism for four subsectors; Table 2 extends to include inter\-basin transfer as a fifth domain\. The isomorphism implies that methods developed in canal automation—where the most mature control theory exists—are systematically transferable to hydropower cascade scheduling, urban pressure management, navigation waterway regulation, and inter\-basin transfer coordination\.

__4  The Unified Model Hierarchy__

The structural isomorphism of Proposition 1 establishes that all water systems share the same mathematical form\. A natural question follows: at what level of model complexity should control be designed? The answer is not a single level but a hierarchy\. This section develops the unified model hierarchy—the mathematical backbone of CHS—establishing that all existing low\-order hydrodynamic models used across water infrastructure, from the Muskingum method in watershed hydrology to the IDZ model in canal automation to the compliance model in pressurized networks, are special cases of a single parametric transfer function family, distinguished only by physical parameter settings and the nature of the downstream boundary condition\.

__4\.1  The Diffusion Wave: Common Ancestor of All Low\-Order Models__

The one\-dimensional Saint\-Venant equations govern unsteady flow in open channels\. The full momentum equation includes local inertia \(∂Q/∂t\), convective inertia \(∂\(Q²/A\)/∂x\), the pressure gradient \(gA∂h/∂x\), gravity \(gAS₀\), and friction \(gASᶠ\)\. For pressurized systems, the water hammer equations \(Wylie & Streeter, 1993\) serve the same role, with piezometric head H replacing depth h and acoustic wave speed a replacing the gravity wave celerity c\.

The diffusion wave approximation, introduced by Hayami \(1951\), drops both inertia terms from the momentum equation, retaining only the balance between friction slope and water surface slope: Sᶠ = S₀ − ∂h/∂x\. Combined with the continuity equation and linearized about a reference state \(Q₀, A₀\), this yields the advection\-diffusion PDE:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(1\)

where c = dQ/dA is the Seddon kinematic wave celerity \(equal to \(5/3\)V₀ for Manning friction in wide channels\), and D is the hydraulic diffusivity, derived by Hayami \(1951\) as:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(2\)

where q = Q₀/B₀ is the unit\-width discharge and S₀ is the bed slope\. This single PDE is the common ancestor from which all low\-order water system models descend\. The Muskingum\-Cunge method emerges as its finite\-difference discretization \(Cunge, 1969\); the Hayami kernel is its analytical impulse response; and the IDZ model emerges from its frequency\-domain approximation for bounded canal pools \(Litrico & Fromion, 2004, 2009\)\. What has not been previously recognized is that these connections establish a single parametric transfer function family that subsumes all existing low\-order models across all water subsectors\.

__4\.2  Two Families, One Physics: Integrating and Self\-Regulating Processes__

The fundamental insight of the CHS unified hierarchy is that all water system transfer functions belong to one of two dual families, distinguished by a single physical property: whether the downstream outflow depends on storage level \(self\-regulating\) or is controlled externally by a gate or pump \(non\-self\-regulating\)\. This distinction, while elementary from a process control perspective, has never been formally recognized as the organizing principle that unifies water system models across subsectors\.

__*Definition 3 \(Non\-self\-regulating water process\)\. *__A water subsystem is non\-self\-regulating if its outflow is determined by an external actuator \(gate opening, valve position, pump speed\) rather than by the system state \(water level, pressure head\)\. In such systems, a persistent flow imbalance ΔQ = Qᵢₙ − Qₒᵤₜ causes the state \(level or pressure\) to ramp indefinitely\. The transfer function has a pole at s = 0 \(integrator\)\.

__*Definition 4 \(Self\-regulating water process\)\. *__A water subsystem is self\-regulating if its outflow increases with storage through a natural resistance relationship \(Manning equation, weir curve, orifice equation, rating curve\)\. In such systems, a persistent flow imbalance is self\-correcting: rising level increases outflow until a new equilibrium is reached\. The transfer function has a finite stable pole at s = −1/Kₛ\.

We now state the central mathematical result of CHS\.

__*Theorem 2 \(Unified Transfer Function Family\)\. *__All single\-input\-single\-output \(SISO\) linear time\-invariant \(LTI\) low\-order models used for control design of one\-dimensional water conveyance and distribution systems are special cases of one of two dual parametric transfer function families, each defined by at most three physical parameters \(effective storage area or time constant, transport delay, lead time constant\):

__*Family α \(Non\-self\-regulating\): *__G\(s\) = \(1 \+ τₘs\) · e^\(−τᵈs\) / \(Aₛ · s\), where Aₛ is the effective storage area \(m²\), τᵈ is the transport delay \(s\), and τₘ is the zero time constant \(s\)\. The integrator pole at s = 0 reflects the non\-self\-regulating nature\. This family governs gated canal pools, pumped pipeline zones, and any subsystem with externally controlled outflow\.

__*Family β \(Self\-regulating\): *__H\(s\) = \(1 − τₘʹs\) · e^\(−τᵈʹs\) / \(1 \+ Kₛs\), where Kₛ is the storage time constant \(s\), τᵈʹ is the transport delay \(s\), and τₘʹ is the lead time constant \(s\)\. The negative sign in the numerator creates a right\-half\-plane zero \(non\-minimum phase behavior—initial inverse response\)\. The stable pole at s = −1/Kₛ reflects the self\-regulating nature\. This family governs natural river reaches, reservoir spillway systems, and any subsystem where outflow increases with storage through a rating curve\.

The two families are not independent—they are dual representations of the same underlying physics, related by the downstream boundary condition\. We establish this through two lemmas and a corollary\.

__*Lemma 1 \(Subsumption of existing models\)\. *__The following established models from four water infrastructure domains are special parameter settings of Families α and β:

The proof for each row is by direct derivation from the governing equations of the respective domain, as established in the originating references\. What is novel is the recognition that all rows are parameter specializations of two families rather than independent models\. □

__*Lemma 2 \(Nash cascade limit; classical, restated in CHS context\)\. *__The Nash cascade of n identical linear reservoirs, each with storage constant K, converges to a pure transport delay as n → ∞ with nK = τᵈ held constant: lim \[1/\(1 \+ τᵈs/n\)\]^n = e^\(−τᵈs\) as n → ∞\.

Proof\. Taking the natural logarithm: ln Hₙ\(s\) = −n · ln\(1 \+ τᵈs/n\)\. For large n, ln\(1 \+ τᵈs/n\) ≈ τᵈs/n − \(τᵈs\)²/\(2n²\) \+ \.\.\., so −n · ln\(1 \+ τᵈs/n\) → −τᵈs\. Therefore Hₙ\(s\) → e^\(−τᵈs\)\. This is the classical result \(1 \+ x/n\)^\(−n\) → e^\(−x\), establishing that distributed storage \(many small reservoirs\) is mathematically equivalent to lumped transport delay—a result that connects the Nash cascade in watershed hydrology to the transport delay in canal control through a rigorous mathematical limit\. □

__4\.3  The Muskingum–IDZ Bridge: Proof of Cross\-Domain Duality__

The deepest result in the unified hierarchy is the exact mathematical relationship between the two families\. This bridge, established by Bolea, Puig and Grau \(2014\) and here formalized as a CHS corollary, proves that the Muskingum model and the IDZ model are not competing descriptions from different disciplines but dual representations of the same physics under different boundary conditions\.

__*Corollary 1 \(Muskingum–IDZ duality\)\. *__When a Family α \(non\-self\-regulating\) canal pool with IDZ transfer function G\(s\) = \(1 \+ τₘs\) · e^\(−τᵈs\) / \(Aₛ · s\) is closed with a linearized self\-regulating downstream boundary Qₒᵤₜ = λy \(where λ is the rating curve gain, e\.g\. spillway coefficient\), the resulting Qᵢₙ → Qₒᵤₜ transfer function is a Family β model\. Specifically, the first\-order MacLaurin approximation of the delay yields the Muskingum transfer function H\(s\) = \(1 − KXs\)/\(1 \+ K\(1−X\)s\) with K = Aₛ/λ and X = λτᵈ/Aₛ\.

Proof\. The closed\-loop transfer function from Qᵢₙ to Qₒᵤₜ with Qₒᵤₜ = λ · y is Gᶜₗ\(s\) = λG\(s\)/\(1 \+ λG\(s\)\)\. Substituting G\(s\) and simplifying:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Applying the first\-order MacLaurin approximation e^\(−τᵈs\) ≈ 1 − τᵈs and neglecting the backwater zero \(τₘ ≈ 0 for simplicity\):

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Rearranging and defining K = Aₛ/λ:

![](data:image/png;base64,)

with the identification X = τᵈ/K = λτᵈ/Aₛ\. This is precisely the Muskingum transfer function derived in watershed hydrology from the storage equation S = K\[XI \+ \(1−X\)Q\] \(Cunge, 1969\)\. The Muskingum weighting factor X, traditionally treated as a calibration parameter in hydrology, is thus revealed to be the ratio of transport delay to total storage time constant: X = τᵈ/\(Aₛ/λ\)\. When X → 0, delay is negligible relative to storage \(pure reservoir\), recovering the linear reservoir model\. When X → 0\.5, the first\-order Padé approximation of a pure delay is recovered\. Note that the duality is approximate: it relies on the MacLaurin truncation of the delay \(valid at low frequencies where τᵈs ≪ 1\) and the neglect of the backwater zero\. The approximation quality degrades at frequencies above 1/τᵈ, i\.e\., at time scales shorter than the transport delay\. For control design purposes, this low\-frequency regime is precisely where the model is applied \(Theorem 3\), so the duality is operationally exact within its intended scope\. □

This result has profound implications for cross\-sector learning\. The Muskingum model, used in every hydrological textbook and flood routing software worldwide \(Chow et al\., 1988\), has been taught for seven decades as an empirical storage\-weighted routing method\. The IDZ model, developed independently by Schuurmans \(1997\) and Litrico and Fromion \(2004\) from frequency\-domain analysis of the Saint\-Venant equations, has been the workhorse of canal automation for two decades\. CHS reveals through Corollary 1 that these are not separate models but the same physics viewed through different downstream boundary conditions—one of the clearest possible demonstrations that disciplinary fragmentation \(Section 2\.2\) has concealed mathematical unity\.

This duality also has a physical interpretation through the Cunge \(1969\) analysis\. Cunge showed that the Muskingum routing equation is the finite\-difference discretization of the diffusion wave PDE \(Equation 1\), with K = Δx/c and X = ½\(1 − q/\(S₀cΔx\)\)\. The parameter X encodes the ratio of physical diffusion D = q/\(2S₀\) to numerical diffusion cΔx/2\. When X = 0\.5 \(zero physical diffusion\), the scheme is pure kinematic wave translation\. When X = 0 \(maximum physical diffusion relative to grid\), the scheme is a pure linear reservoir\. The Muskingum parameters are not free calibration constants—they are determined by channel physics\. CHS provides the unifying framework within which the Cunge finite\-difference route and the Litrico\-Fromion frequency\-domain route converge on the same parametric family\.

__4\.4  The Pipe Compliance Integrator: Elastic Storage as Gravitational Storage__

For pressurized water distribution systems, the water hammer equations \(Wylie & Streeter, 1993; Chaudhry, 2014\) are the distributed\-parameter governing dynamics, playing the same role as the Saint\-Venant equations for open channels\. When the pipe length L is short relative to the wavelength of pressure fluctuations of interest \(a lumped approximation valid at the time scales of pressure control\), the distributed equations reduce to a single hydraulic capacitance:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(3\)

where H is piezometric head, Qᵈₑₘₐₙᵈ is the time\-varying demand disturbance, and the hydraulic capacitance is:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(4\)

Here g is gravitational acceleration, A is the pipe cross\-sectional area, L is the effective pipe length, and a is the pressure wave speed given by a² = \(Kᶠ/ρ\)/\[1 \+ \(KᶠDₚ\)/\(Ee\)\], where Kᶠ is the fluid bulk modulus \(≈2\.15 GPa for water\), ρ is fluid density, E is the pipe Young’s modulus, e is the wall thickness, and Dₚ is the pipe diameter \(Ghidaoui et al\., 2005\)\. The transfer function is:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(5\)

This is a pure integrator—structurally identical to the canal Integrator model G\(s\) = 1/\(Aₛ · s\)\. The correspondence is physically revealing: the canal backwater area Aₛ represents gravitational storage capacity \(a free\-surface area that absorbs flow imbalances by changing water level\), while the pipe hydraulic capacitance Cₕ represents elastic storage capacity \(combined fluid compression and pipe wall expansion that absorbs flow imbalances by changing pressure head\)\. Both are instances of Family α with τₘ = 0, τᵈ = 0, and the effective storage parameter being Aₛ \(canal, m²\) or Cₕ \(pipe, m³/m = m² when expressed per unit head\)\. The key physical difference is the time scale: the much faster wave speed in pressurized systems \(a ≈ 1000 m/s vs\. c ≈ 1 m/s for open channels\) compresses the transport delay from hours to seconds, requiring correspondingly faster sampling for control\.

__4\.5  The Actuator Reduction: Steady\-State Boundary Conditions__

The unified transfer function family \(Theorem 2\) describes how water levels and flows evolve between actuator boundaries—the global dynamics of pools, reaches, and pipe segments\. But every such model requires boundary conditions specifying how flow relates to control inputs \(gate opening, pump speed, valve position, wicket gate angle\) and local heads\. These boundary conditions—the actuator characteristic curves—are themselves products of order reduction: the local momentum or energy equation at each actuator is simplified to a static algebraic map by invoking the same steady\-state assumption that produces Level 1 \(SS\) in the plant hierarchy, but applied locally at the actuator boundary rather than globally across a reach\.

The physical starting point for every water system actuator is Newton’s second law applied to the fluid element accelerating through the constriction or interacting with a rotating machine\. For gates and valves, the unsteady Bernoulli equation along the streamline gives Lₐ\(dv/dt\) \+ ½v² = gΔH, where Lₐ is the effective length of the accelerating water column and ΔH = Hᵤₚ − Hᵈₙ the driving head\. The transient solution v\(t\) = √\(2gΔH\)·tanh\(t/τᶝ\) has a gate water\-column time constant τᶝ = Lₐ/√\(2gΔH\), typically 0\.1–1 s\. For pumps, the Euler turbomachinery equation couples with rotational dynamics J\(dω/dt\) = Tₘₒₜₒᵣ − Tₕᵧᵈ, where the mechanical time constant Tₘ = Jω₀/T₀ is typically 2–10 s\. For turbines, the penstock rigid water column equation Tᵥ\(dq/dt\) = h₀ − h − f\(q\) introduces the water starting time Tᵥ = LQ₀/\(gAH₀\), typically 0\.5–4 s, yielding the non\-minimum\-phase transfer function Gₚ\(s\) = \(1 − Tᵥs\)/\(1 \+ 0\.5Tᵥs\) for the linearized ideal turbine \(Kundur, 1994; IEEE Working Group, 1992\)\.

Setting all time derivatives to zero eliminates these fast local dynamics, producing a static nonlinear map Q = f\(u, Hᵤₚ, Hᵈₙ\) for each actuator type: the orifice equation Q = Cᵈ·w·u·√\(2gΔH\) for sluice gates \(Henderson, 1966\), the pump characteristic H = αN² \+ βNQ \+ γQ² with affinity laws for variable\-speed pumps, the valve equation Q = Cᵥ\(u\)·√\(ΔP/ρ\) with inherent characteristics \(linear, equal\-percentage, or quick\-opening\) per ISA\-75\.01, and the turbine Hill chart Q = Q₁₁\(n₁₁, α\)·D²√H which at synchronous speed simplifies to Q = G√H—exactly the orifice equation\. We formalize this observation\.

__*Lemma 3 \(Unified Actuator Characteristic\)\. *__Every water system actuator—gate, pump, valve, or turbine—when modeled under the quasi\-steady \(zero\-inertia\) assumption, produces a static nonlinear map Q = f\(u, Hᵤₚ, Hᵈₙ\)\. Linearization about an operating point \(Q₀, u₀, H₀\) yields the universal three\-term boundary condition:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(6\)

where α = ∂Q/∂u is the actuator gain, βᵤₚ = ∂Q/∂Hᵤₚ, and βᵈₙ = ∂Q/∂Hᵈₙ\. For all orifice\-type actuators \(gates, valves, turbines at fixed speed\), βᵈₙ = −βᵤₚ by antisymmetry of the ΔH dependence, and βᵤₚ = Q₀/\(2ΔH₀\) universally, reflecting the √\(ΔH\) structure common to all\. The time\-scale separation justifying this reduction is quantitative: the eliminated actuator dynamics \(0\.1–10 s\) are two to three orders of magnitude faster than the retained plant dynamics \(100–10,000 s for canal pools; 10–1,000 s for pipe networks\)\. This ratio ensures the actuator reaches its new equilibrium before the plant can respond appreciably\. The quasi\-steady assumption fails only during emergency transients \(water hammer from rapid gate closure, pump trip\) where the Joukowsky pressure surge ΔH = a·V/g must be captured—but these are precisely the events handled by Layer 0 \(Safety\) using the full Level 5 model \(Theorem 3\), not the control\-design levels\.

This actuator reduction is the second instance of the order\-reduction principle \(P3\) applied in the CHS framework\. The first, developed in Sections 4\.1–4\.4, reduces the global plant dynamics \(Saint\-Venant PDE → transfer function → integrator → steady state\)\. The second, formalized here, reduces the local actuator dynamics \(unsteady Bernoulli/Euler → static characteristic curve → linearized gains\)\. The two reductions are consistent because the time scales nest cleanly: τₐᶜₜᵤₐₜₒᵣ ≪ τᵥₐᵥₑ ≪ τₚₒₒₗ\. Together, the global plant transfer function \(Theorem 2\) and the local actuator algebraic boundary condition \(Lemma 3\) provide a complete, modular description of any water control system: swap in any actuator type by substituting \(α, βᵤₚ, βᵈₙ\) without altering the plant model structure\.

__4\.6  The Five\-Level Hierarchy: A Principled Reduction Path__

We now formalize the five\-level hierarchy as a sequence of mathematically principled reductions from the full PDE dynamics to algebraic balance\. Each level is obtained from the one above by a specific simplification—linearization, zero neglect, delay neglect, or steady\-state assumption—and each discards dynamics operating at time scales faster than the corresponding control function requires\. For the non\-self\-regulating family \(Family α\), which governs most controlled water infrastructure:

__Level 5 — Linearized Saint\-Venant \(LSV\)\. __The full linearized one\-dimensional unsteady flow equations with wave speeds c± = v ± √\(gA/T\)\. For pressurized systems: water hammer equations with wave speed a\. Infinite\-dimensional; equivalent to the diffusion wave PDE \(Equation 1\) when inertia is secondary\. Valid at all time scales; used for safety verification\.

__Level 4 — Integrator\-Delay\-Zero \(IDZ\)\. __G\(s\) = \(1 \+ τₘs\) · e^\(−τᵈs\) / \(Aₛ · s\)\. Three physically meaningful parameters derived from low\-frequency approximation \(Litrico & Fromion, 2004\)\. Self\-regulating dual: Muskingum H\(s\) = \(1 − KXs\)/\(1 \+ K\(1−X\)s\), via Corollary 1\. Third\-order after Padé approximation\. Valid at minutes\-to\-hours; used for pool\-level regulation \(Layer 1\)\.

__Level 3 — Integrator\-Delay \(ID\)\. __G\(s\) = e^\(−τᵈs\) / \(Aₛ · s\)\. Neglects backwater zero \(τₘ = 0\)\. Introduced by Schuurmans \(1997\); equivalent to IPDT in process control\. Self\-regulating dual: FOPDT\. Cunge \(1969\) showed this structure is the diffusion wave PDE discretized with K = Δx/c, X = ½\(1 − q/\(S₀cΔx\)\)\. Valid at hours\.

__Level 2 — Integrator \(I\) / Linear Reservoir \(LR\)\. __G\(s\) = 1/\(Aₛ · s\) or H\(s\) = 1/\(1\+Ks\)\. Neglects delay \(τᵈ = 0\)\. Family α: reservoir continuity dV/dt = Qᵢₙ − Qₒᵤₜ, pipe compliance Cₕ·dH/dt = ΔQ\. Family β: Nash linear reservoir S = KQ\. Lemma 2 shows n cascaded reservoirs converge to pure delay as n → ∞\. First\-order; valid at hours\-to\-days; used for coordination \(Layer 2\)\.

__Level 1 — Steady\-State Mass Balance \(SS\)\. __Sets dV/dt = 0, yielding Qᵢₙ = Qₒᵤₜ \+ Qₗₒₛₛ\. Zero\-order \(no dynamics\)\. The level at which conventional water resources systems analysis operates \(Loucks & van Beek, 2017\)\. Valid at days\-to\-seasons; used for planning\.

The reduction path LSV → IDZ → ID → I → SS is not arbitrary; each step is a mathematically principled operation\. The self\-regulating branch follows a parallel path: diffusion wave PDE → Muskingum \(lead\-lag\) → FOPDT → linear reservoir → steady\-state rating curve\. Figure 2 illustrates the complete dual hierarchy\.

__*\[Figure 2 about here\]*__

__4\.7  From Saint\-Venant to State Space: The IDZ Derivation__

The derivation of the IDZ model proceeds through four steps, following Litrico and Fromion \(2004, 2009\)\. Step 1: Linearization of the Saint\-Venant equations around steady\-state uniform flow \(Q₀, y₀\), yielding linear hyperbolic PDEs\. Boundary conditions are the linearized actuator characteristic \(Lemma 3\): qᵤ\(t\) = αᵤΔuᵤ\(t\) \+ βᵤΔy\(0,t\) at x = 0 and qᵈ\(t\) = αᵈΔuᵈ\(t\) \+ βᵈΔy\(L,t\) at x = L\. Step 2: Laplace transform converts PDEs to ODEs in s, with solutions as 2×2 transfer matrices\. The key result of Litrico and Fromion \(2004\) is that the downstream\-level\-to\-upstream\-flow element p₁₁\(s\), despite involving irrational hyperbolic functions, admits a low\-frequency rational approximation\. Step 3: IDZ approximation at low frequencies: G\(s\) ≈ \(1/Aₛ\)\(1 \+ τₘs\)/\(s · e^\(−τᵈs\)\), with Aₛ ≈ T₀L, τᵈ ≈ L/\(v₀ \+ c₀\), and τₘ ≈ L/\(2c₀\)\. Step 4: Padé approximation e^\(−τᵈs\) ≈ \(1 − τᵈs/2\)/\(1 \+ τᵈs/2\) and discretization at sampling period Tₛ yield x\(k\+1\) = Ax\(k\) \+ Bu\(k\) \+ Bᵈd\(k\), y\(k\) = Cx\(k\), with 3×3 state vector x = \[pool volume deviation; delayed input; Padé auxiliary\]ᵀ\.

This four\-step chain—linearization, Laplace transform, rational approximation, discretization—is the canonical CHS derivation for Level 4 models\. The Cunge \(1969\) route provides an alternative for the self\-regulating branch: finite\-difference discretization of the diffusion wave PDE \(Equation 1\) with numerical diffusion matching\. Both routes converge on the unified family \(Theorem 2\)\.

__4\.8  Model–Layer Correspondence__

__*Theorem 3 \(Model–Layer Correspondence\)\. *__In a CHS\-compliant control architecture, each control layer shall use a model of sufficient fidelity for its temporal scope and no more:

__\(i\) Layer 0 \(Safety\): __millisecond\-to\-second response\. Level 5 \(LSV\) for offline verification; hardwired interlocks for runtime\. No model\-based computation in the critical path\.

__\(ii\) Layer 1 \(Regulation\): __minute\-scale response\. Level 4 \(IDZ or Muskingum, per boundary type\) as internal model for MPC or LQR\. Captures dominant dynamics while remaining tractable for real\-time constrained optimization\.

__\(iii\) Layer 2 \(Coordination\): __hour\-scale response\. Level 2 \(I or LR\) coupled through mass balance at junctions\. Transport delays negligible at this temporal scope\.

__\(iv\) Planning Layer: __day\-to\-week scale\. Level 1 \(SS\)—algebraic mass balance \(Loucks & van Beek, 2017\)\.

The correspondence applies identically across subsectors via the unified family\. For pressurized networks: water hammer → linearized network → quasi\-steady with delay → compliance integrator → steady\-state allocation\. For reservoir systems: 2D hydrodynamic → 1D routing → Muskingum → storage continuity → water balance\. Theorem 2 guarantees this universality\. Horváth et al\. \(2024\) recently demonstrated automatic model structure selection for canal control without manual tuning, empirically validating the model hierarchy: their algorithm recovers the IDZ structure when data support it and degrades gracefully to ID or I when they do not—exactly the behavior predicted by the CHS reduction path\.

__*\[Figure 3 about here\]*__

__5  The Eight Governing Principles__

Building on the formalization of Sections 3–4, we identify eight principles governing water system operations\. The preliminary CHS framework \(Lei, 2025a\) identified feedback and decoupling as two foundational principles\. Here we expand to eight, derived from systematic enumeration of four design dimensions—temporal, spatial, complexity, and systemic—each requiring both an operational mechanism and a resilience mechanism\. The temporal dimension yields Feedback \(P1\) and Adaptation \(P7\); the spatial dimension yields Decoupling \(P2\) and Coordination \(P6\); the complexity dimension yields Order Reduction \(P3\) and Robustness \(P5\); the systemic dimension yields Emergence \(P4\) and Hierarchy \(P8\)\. This 4×2 structure provides a completeness argument: the eight principles are organized into an Operational Tetrad and a Resilience Tetrad, The four dimensions correspond to the four fundamental design degrees of freedom in any distributed control system: when to act \(temporal\), where to act \(spatial\), how much detail to model \(complexity\), and how to compose local decisions into global behavior \(systemic\)\. Each dimension requires both a mechanism for normal operation and a mechanism for maintaining performance under uncertainty, yielding the 4×2 structure\. We acknowledge that an ‘informational’ dimension \(data quality, communication bandwidth\) could be argued as a fifth; we subsume it under the temporal \(sampling\) and spatial \(communication topology\) dimensions, but recognize this as a design choice rather than a mathematical necessity\.

__*\[Figure 4 about here\]*__

__5\.1  The Operational Tetrad__

__*5\.1\.1  Principle 1: Feedback*__

Feedback—continuously measuring system state and adjusting control actions to reduce discrepancy from desired states—is foundational\. Without feedback, water system operation is open\-loop scheduling: a pre\-computed plan executed without regard to actual system response\. Two factors amplify the necessity of feedback in water systems: disturbances are large and poorly predictable \(inflows varying by orders of magnitude\), and long transport delays mean consequences of errors accumulate far downstream\. CHS emphasizes multi\-scale feedback: fast local loops for safety \(seconds\), medium\-speed loops for pool\-level regulation \(minutes\), and slow outer loops for coordination \(hours\), as recognized by Clemmens and Schuurmans \(2004\)\. Water systems impose a specific constraint absent from most process control: the ratio of transport delay to dominant time constant, τᵈ/Kₛ, is typically 0\.3–0\.8—far larger than in chemical process control where τᵈ/Kₛ < 0\.1 is common \(Seborg et al\., 2011\)\. This large delay ratio severely limits achievable closed\-loop bandwidth and demands model\-predictive \(rather than purely reactive\) feedback architectures\.

__*5\.1\.2  Principle 2: Decoupling*__

Water networks are inherently coupled: a gate adjustment propagates both upstream \(backwater\) and downstream \(flow disturbance\), creating cascade effects across interconnected pools\. The decoupling principle requires minimizing inter\-subsystem disturbance propagation through local volume compensation\. Litrico and Fromion \(2009\) demonstrated that downstream control inherently provides better decoupling by exploiting pool storage as a buffer\. CHS generalizes: in any water network, natural storage elements \(canal pools, reservoir zones, pipeline elastic capacity\) should be systematically exploited as local disturbance absorbers \(Lei, 2025a\)\. Quantitatively, a pool with backwater area Aₛ can absorb a flow disturbance ΔQ for a duration Tₛᵤᶠ = Aₛ·Δyₘₐₓ/ΔQ before reaching constraint limits—the ‘decoupling time horizon\.’ This horizon determines the minimum coordination update frequency: if Tᶜₒₘₘ > Tₛᵤᶠ, the pool saturates before the coordinator can respond\.

__*5\.1\.3  Principle 3: Order Reduction*__

The unified model hierarchy of Section 4 is the direct expression of this principle\. Order reduction addresses the gap between PDE\-level dynamics \(∞\-dimensional\) and real\-time computational requirements\. The five\-level hierarchy \(LSV→IDZ→ID→I→SS\) with its unified transfer function family \(Theorem 2\) provides a principled reduction path, where each level is a specific parameter specialization of the same three\-parameter family\. The key insight is that different control functions require different model fidelities, and that the downstream boundary condition determines which branch \(Family α integrating or Family β self\-regulating\) applies—the selection governed by Theorem 3\. The principle operates recursively at two scales: globally across reaches \(Section 4\.1–4\.4\) and locally at each actuator boundary \(Section 4\.5\), where unsteady momentum equations are reduced to static characteristic curves with time\-scale separation ratios of 100–10,000\.

__*5\.1\.4  Principle 4: Emergence*__

Emergence refers to system\-level behaviors arising from interactions among locally controlled subsystems\. In water networks, emergence can be positive—autonomous pool controllers achieving network\-wide flow balance without explicit central coordination—or negative—individually stable controllers producing network\-level oscillations through hydrodynamic coupling\. Multi\-agent systems theory \(Wooldridge, 2009\) provides the analytical framework\. The design challenge is defining local interaction rules that guarantee desirable emergent behavior, connecting to consensus algorithms and distributed optimization \(Nedić & Ozdaglar, 2009\)\. Water networks exhibit a specific emergence pathology: downstream controllers, by rejecting disturbances back upstream, can create inter\-pool oscillations whose period scales as 2Στᵈᵢ—the sum of transport delays along the cascade\. This ‘hydraulic resonance’ is unique to spatially distributed flow systems and has no direct analog in electrical power grids or chemical process networks\.

__5\.2  The Resilience Tetrad__

__*5\.2\.1  Principle 5: Robustness*__

Robustness maintains acceptable performance despite uncertainties in the plant model, sensor measurements, and disturbance forecasts\. In water systems, channel roughness changes with sediment deposition, sensor calibration drifts, and hydrological forecasts carry substantial errors beyond 24–48 hours\. Schuurmans \(1997\) was among the first to apply robust control theory to canal regulation\. CHS elevates robustness from a property of individual controllers to a system\-level architectural requirement\.

__*5\.2\.2  Principle 6: Coordination*__

Coordination aligns distributed controllers for system\-wide objectives under constraints of spatial distribution, limited communication bandwidth, and jurisdictional boundaries\. CHS frames this through distributed MPC: each subsystem solves a local optimization while exchanging boundary information with neighbors \(Negenborn et al\., 2009; Maestre & Negenborn, 2014\)\. The South\-to\-North Water Diversion Middle Route, with 64 check gates over 1,432 km, exemplifies the need: centralized MPC is computationally intractable at this scale\.

__*5\.2\.3  Principle 7: Adaptation*__

Adaptation modifies control behavior when operating conditions exceed the design envelope\. The Operational Design Domain \(ODD\) concept from autonomous vehicles \(SAE International, 2021; ISO, 2022\) is central to CHS: for each autonomy level, the conditions for autonomous operation are explicitly defined, and the system transitions to lower automation or human control at ODD boundaries\. The autonomous water network architecture \(Lei, 2025b\), defining Water Network Intelligence Levels WN\-L0 through WN\-L5, operationalizes this principle\.

__*5\.2\.4  Principle 8: Hierarchy*__

Hierarchy organizes the control system in multiple layers: Layer 0 \(Safety\)—local PLCs providing interlocks at millisecond response without requiring communication; Layer 1 \(Regulation\)—pool\-level MPC at minute\-scale; Layer 2 \(Coordination\)—system\-wide optimization at hourly scale\. This mirrors the ISA\-95 industrial automation model, the primary/secondary/tertiary frequency control hierarchy in power systems, and the stability augmentation/autopilot/flight management hierarchy in aerospace\. CHS formalizes this specifically for water networks, defining information interfaces between layers and specifying graceful degradation requirements: each layer must maintain safety autonomously if communication with higher layers is lost—a direct consequence of OS5\.

__5\.3  Inter\-Principle Tradeoffs__

A critical feature distinguishing CHS from a mere taxonomy is that the eight principles exhibit fundamental tradeoffs defining the feasible design space\. We identify four primary tensions:

__*Feedback–Robustness tension \(P1–P5\)\. *__Faster feedback improves disturbance rejection but amplifies sensor noise and model uncertainty\. In water systems with large transport delays, aggressive feedback gains can destabilize the control loop \(Schuurmans, 1997\)\. The resolution lies in model\-based feedback \(MPC\) that explicitly accounts for delay and uncertainty, rather than high\-gain reactive control\.

__*Decoupling–Coordination tension \(P2–P6\)\. *__Perfect decoupling eliminates disturbance propagation but sacrifices global optimality—water stored locally for decoupling is unavailable for system\-wide redistribution\. Perfect coordination requires centralized optimization, which is computationally intractable and vulnerable to communication failure\. The resolution is hierarchical DMPC: strong decoupling at Layer 1 combined with loose coordination at Layer 2\.

__*Order Reduction–Robustness tension \(P3–P5\)\. *__More aggressive model simplification enables faster computation but introduces larger modeling errors\. The IDZ model neglects high\-frequency dynamics; using it for fast safety protection may miss rapid transients\. CHS resolves this through scale\-appropriate model selection \(Theorem 3\): Level 5 for safety verification, Level 4 for regulation, Level 2 for coordination\.

__*Emergence–Hierarchy tension \(P4–P8\)\. *__Greater local autonomy reduces communication requirements and increases resilience, but decreases system\-level predictability\. Stronger hierarchical control provides tighter performance guarantees but creates single points of failure\. CHS advocates ‘residual autonomy’: hierarchical coordination under normal conditions, with graceful degradation to emergent local control when communication is impaired—a direct consequence of OS5\.

These tradeoffs interact: the Feedback–Robustness tension couples with Order Reduction–Robustness through internal model choice, and Decoupling–Coordination couples with Emergence–Hierarchy through communication architecture\. A complete CHS design navigates this multi\-dimensional tradeoff space, with the operational singularity \(Definition 1\) providing the ultimate criterion: any configuration that risks constraint violation under plausible uncertainty is inadmissible, regardless of performance optimality\.

__*Quantitative illustration: the P2–P6 tradeoff\.*__ The Decoupling–Coordination tradeoff admits analytical treatment\. Consider a single pool with storage capacity V\_total, transport delay τᵈ, and coordination update interval T\_comm\. Define the buffer fraction f\_b = V\_buffer/V\_total as the fraction of storage reserved for local disturbance absorption \(decoupling\)\. For a step disturbance ΔQ, the pool can absorb ΔQ·τᵈ of volumetric disturbance before the wave transit is complete\. If the coordination cycle T\_comm > τᵈ, the pool must buffer the full disturbance autonomously until the coordinator responds, requiring f\_b ≥ ΔQ·T\_comm/\(V\_total·Δy\_max/y\_range\)\. Under simplified assumptions \(constant disturbance amplitude, single\-pool\), the optimal buffer fraction follows: f\_b\* ≈ min\(1, τᵈ/T\_comm\)\. When τᵈ/T\_comm > 1 \(slow coordination relative to wave transit\), nearly all storage must serve local buffering \(f\_b → 1\)\. When τᵈ/T\_comm → 0 \(fast coordination\), minimal local buffering is needed and storage is freed for system\-wide redistribution \(f\_b → 0\)\. This derivation provides the analytical basis for Prediction 3 \(Section 9\.2\)\. In practice, DMPC coordination overhead and multi\-pool coupling introduce a penalty factor that shifts the curve upward, requiring numerical simulation for precise optimization \(Section 6\.2\)\.

__6  Illustrative Applications__

To demonstrate that CHS is an operational framework and not merely a conceptual taxonomy, we present three applications of increasing complexity: single\-pool LQR feedback design, multi\-pool distributed MPC, and cross\-sector transfer from canal to reservoir to urban pressure zone\. The results presented are analytical predictions derived from the linear reduced\-order models of Section 4; full nonlinear simulation validation against Saint\-Venant benchmarks is deferred to a companion computational paper\.

__6\.1  Single Canal Pool: IDZ Model and LQR Feedback Design__

Consider a single trapezoidal canal pool of length L = 10 km, controlled by an upstream gate \(inflow Qᵢₙ\) and a downstream gate \(outflow Qₒᵤₜ\), with a target downstream water level yᵣᵉᶠ\. Following the derivation chain of Section 4\.2, the Saint\-Venant dynamics are reduced to the IDZ transfer function \(Level 4\):

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(7\)

For a typical pool \(slope S₀ = 0\.0001, Manning n = 0\.016, base flow Q₀ = 30 m³/s, trapezoidal section with bottom width 10 m\), the characteristic parameters are Aₛ ≈ 85,000 m², τᵈ ≈ 1,800 s, and τₘ ≈ 600 s\. Using Padé approximation and discretizing at Tₛ = 300 s:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(8\)

with a 3×3 state vector x = \[pool volume deviation; delayed input state; Padé auxiliary state\]ᵀ\. The resulting discrete A matrix has eigenvalues at approximately 1\.0, 0\.85, and 0\.72—the unit eigenvalue reflects the integrator, confirming marginal stability without feedback\.

The feedback principle \(P1\) is operationalized through linear quadratic regulator \(LQR\) design, minimizing the cost:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(9\)

With Q = diag\(1, 0, 0\) and R = 0\.01, the optimal gain K shifts closed\-loop eigenvalues to approximately 0\.92, 0\.78, and 0\.65—all inside the unit circle, confirming asymptotic stability\. The settling time is approximately 4,000 s \(70 minutes\) with less than 5% overshoot and peak water level deviation of 0\.08 m for a step disturbance of 2 m³/s, consistent with published canal control benchmarks \(Clemmens & Schuurmans, 2004\)\.

__6\.2  Multi\-Pool Extension: Distributed MPC__

A single canal pool rarely operates in isolation\. Consider a series of n pools with n\+1 gates, where pool i has state xᵢ, upstream gate input uᵢ, and downstream disturbance dᵢ = uᵢ₊₁ \(the next gate’s release becomes this pool’s outflow disturbance\)\. The coupled system state is x = \[x₁, \.\.\., xₙ\]ᵀ ∈ ℝ³ⁿ with control u = \[u₁, \.\.\., uₙ₊₁\]ᵀ ∈ ℝⁿ⁺¹\.

A centralized MPC solving all n pools jointly requires a QP with O\(3n\) states and O\(n\) controls over prediction horizon N, yielding O\(nN\) decision variables and O\(nN\) constraints\. The computational complexity of the QP solver scales as O\(\(nN\)³\), which for the South\-to\-North Water Diversion Middle Route \(n = 64, N = 12\) involves approximately 2,300 decision variables and 13,800 constraints—solvable in principle but challenging for guaranteed real\-time response at 300 s sampling\.

Distributed MPC \(DMPC\), implementing the coordination principle \(P6\), decomposes the problem\. Each pool i solves a local MPC with O\(3\) states and O\(1\) control over horizon N, yielding O\(N\) decision variables\. The pools exchange only boundary information—the planned upstream discharge trajectory uᵢ\(k|k\), \.\.\., uᵢ\(k\+N|k\)—with their downstream neighbor\. The coordination protocol proceeds iteratively: \(i\) each pool solves its local MPC assuming the last received neighbor trajectories; \(ii\) boundary trajectories are exchanged; \(iii\) steps \(i\)–\(ii\) repeat until convergence or a maximum iteration count\. The per\-pool complexity is O\(N³\), and the total complexity is O\(n · N³ · J\) where J is the number of coordination iterations—typically 3–5 for practical convergence \(Negenborn et al\., 2009\)\. For n = 64 and N = 12, this reduces computation by approximately two orders of magnitude versus centralized MPC while providing near\-optimal performance\.

The Decoupling–Coordination tradeoff \(P2–P6\) manifests directly: allocating more pool storage to local disturbance buffering \(decoupling\) reduces the coupling terms that coordination must resolve, but decreases the volume available for system\-wide redistribution\. The optimal buffer fraction depends on the ratio τᵈ/Tᶜₒₘₘ, where τᵈ is the pool transport delay and Tᶜₒₘₘ is the coordination update interval \(see Prediction 3 in Section 8\)\. The X\-in\-the\-Loop framework \(Lei, 2025c\) provides the verification methodology for validating DMPC controllers through progressive MiL, SiL, HiL, and PiL testing stages\.

__6\.3  Cross\-Sector Transfer: Canal → Reservoir → Urban Pressure Zone__

Proposition 1 predicts that the same algorithmic structure applies across subsectors upon re\-parameterization\. We verify this for two transfers\.

__*Transfer 1: Canal pool → Reservoir\. *__The reservoir continuity equation dV/dt = Qᵢₙ\(t\) − Qₒᵤₜ\(u, h\) is precisely the Integrator \(Level 2\) model from the hierarchy—a first\-order system with state x = V, control u \(release\), disturbance d = Qᵢₙ, and constraint g = \[hₘᵢₙ − h\(V\); h\(V\) − hₘₐₓ\] ≤ 0:

![](data:image/png;base64,)	\(10\)

The A, B, C matrices become scalars: A = 1, B = −Tₛ/Aₕ \(where Aₕ is reservoir surface area at operating level\), C = 1/Aₕ\. The MPC formulation is identical to Section 6\.1 with θ = \{Aₕ, Qᵢₙ statistics, hₘᵢₙ, hₘₐₓ\} replacing the canal parameters\. No algorithmic modification is required\.

__*Transfer 2: Canal pool → Urban pressure zone\. *__A District Metered Area \(DMA\) in an urban distribution network admits a lumped\-parameter model analogous to the canal pool\. The state variable is pressure head H at the critical node \(analogous to pool water level y\)\. The actuator is a pressure\-reducing valve \(PRV\) or variable\-frequency drive \(VFD\) pump \(analogous to a check gate\)\. The storage capacity is the hydraulic compliance of the pipe network Cₕ = dV/dH \(analogous to backwater area Aₛ\)\. The transport delay is the pressure wave travel time τᵈ = L/a, where a is the water hammer wave speed \(typically 800–1200 m/s, much faster than open\-channel waves\)\. The governing equation is Cₕ · dH/dt = Qᵢₙ − Qᵈₑₘₐₙᵈ\(t\), which is once again the Integrator model with state H, control Qᵢₙ \(pump/valve flow\), and disturbance Qᵈₑₘₐₙᵈ\. The matrices are: A = 1, B = Tₛ/Cₕ, C = 1\. The MPC formulation is algorithmically identical; only the physical parameters change\. The key distinction is the time scale: the much faster wave speed \(a ≈ 1000 m/s vs\. c ≈ 1 m/s\) compresses the transport delay from hours \(canal\) to seconds \(pipe\), requiring correspondingly faster sampling \(Tₛ ≈ 1–10 s\)\.

These three applications—canal pool \(IDZ, Level 4\), reservoir \(I, Level 2\), and urban pressure zone \(I, Level 2 with fast dynamics\)—demonstrate that a single MPC software framework, with subsector\-specific parameter files, can serve across water infrastructure\. This is the concrete operational consequence of structural isomorphism \(Proposition 1, S1–S5\)\.

__7  From Theory to Architecture: The Autonomous Operation Framework__

Sections 2–6 established the theoretical foundations of CHS: operational singularity motivates a dedicated science, structural isomorphism enables cross\-sector unification, the model–control hierarchy provides mathematical tools, principles guide design, and applications demonstrate feasibility\. A natural question follows: how should these theoretical elements be assembled into an implementable system architecture that can progressively advance water infrastructure from manual operation toward autonomy? This section addresses that question by introducing three interlocking concepts—Hierarchical Distributed Control \(HDC\), the Operational Design Domain \(ODD\), and a Multi\-Agent System \(MAS\) architecture—and by defining Water Systems Autonomy Levels \(WSAL\) as the roadmap for the transition\.

__7\.1  Hierarchical Distributed Control: The Physical AI Engine__

The model–layer correspondence \(Theorem 3\) implies a natural control architecture: each layer of the hierarchy—from Layer 0 safety through Layer 3 planning—employs the model of appropriate complexity, coupled with the control algorithm matched to its temporal scope\. We term this Hierarchical Distributed Control \(HDC\)—hierarchical because control decisions are stratified by timescale, and distributed because within each layer, neighboring subsystems coordinate through decoupled yet communicating local controllers \(Principles 2 and 6\)\.

Concretely, HDC consists of four stacked layers operating concurrently\. Layer 0 \(Safety Floor\) implements hard constraint enforcement through programmable logic controllers \(PLCs\) operating at millisecond cycles—gate\-closure interlocks, high\-water\-level alarms, emergency shutdowns—requiring no model beyond threshold logic and executing unconditionally regardless of commands from upper layers\. Layer 1 \(Real\-time Regulation\) deploys MPC with IDZ or Integrator\-Delay internal models at sampling intervals of seconds to minutes, tracking reference trajectories while respecting state and actuator constraints\. Layer 2 \(Coordination\) employs distributed MPC \(Negenborn et al\., 2009; Maestre & Negenborn, 2014\) at minutes\-to\-hours horizons, resolving inter\-pool conflicts through iterative neighbor\-to\-neighbor negotiation using the coordination mechanisms formalized in Principle 6\. Layer 3 \(Planning\) performs nested optimization over day\-to\-year horizons, translating high\-level objectives—seasonal water allocation targets, environmental flow requirements, energy scheduling—into reference trajectories for lower layers using steady\-state or Integrator models\.

The defining characteristic of HDC is that every control action, at every layer, is computed from first\-principles physical models—the CHS model hierarchy of Section 4\. This is why we characterize HDC as the Physical AI engine of the architecture: it is artificial intelligence in the sense of automated decision\-making, but grounded entirely in mechanistic models with provable constraint guarantees rather than learned correlations\. The critical design rule is the Layer 0 veto: no command from any upper layer may override Layer 0 safety interlocks, ensuring that the operational singularity property OS1 \(failure irreversibility\) is respected architecturally, not merely algorithmically\.

__7\.2  Operational Design Domain: Defining the Safety Envelope__

Automotive autonomous driving has formalized a concept of central importance to any safety\-critical automation: the Operational Design Domain \(ODD\)—the specific set of operating conditions under which the automation system is designed to function \(SAE International, 2021\)\. We adapt this concept to water systems and argue that it resolves a fundamental barrier to water automation adoption: the ‘trust gap’ between what automated controllers can theoretically do and what operators are willing to let them do\.

An ODD for a water network segment is defined by a bounded region in a multi\-dimensional operating space: flow range \[Q\_min, Q\_max\], water level range \[h\_min, h\_max\], demand\-disturbance scenarios \(e\.g\., normal delivery, diurnal peak, drought conditions, inter\-basin emergency transfer\), equipment status \(all actuators functional, single actuator failure, communication degradation\), and environmental conditions \(normal weather, storm event, ice formation\)\. Within the certified ODD, the HDC controller has been verified—through the X\-in\-the\-Loop \(xIL\) testing framework \(Lei, 2025c\)—to maintain all constraints while achieving performance targets\. Outside the ODD boundary, control authority reverts to human operators or to a degraded safe mode\.

The ODD concept transforms the question of water automation trust from a binary ‘automate or not’ into a graduated, verifiable framework: for which specific scenarios, under what specific conditions, has this controller been certified? This parallels the automotive progression from highway\-only cruise control \(narrow ODD\) to all\-weather urban driving \(broad ODD\)\. For water systems, a practical implementation starts with a narrow ODD—e\.g\., normal flow delivery with all actuators functional—and progressively expands through systematic xIL testing: Model\-in\-the\-Loop \(MiL\) for algorithm validation, Software\-in\-the\-Loop \(SiL\) for code verification, Hardware\-in\-the\-Loop \(HiL\) for actuator\-communication integration, and Plant\-in\-the\-Loop \(PiL\) for field commissioning \(Lei, 2025c\)\. The analogy to DO\-178C airborne software certification \(RTCA, 2011\) and ISO 26262 functional safety \(ISO, 2018\) is deliberate: the water sector requires comparable rigor for its safety\-critical automation\.

__7\.3  The Multi\-Agent System Architecture__

HDC provides accurate control grounded in physics, and ODD defines the safety envelope\. However, real\-world water networks face a challenge that pure HDC cannot address: scenario transitions that require cognitive judgment\. When a drought escalates from moderate to severe, when a pump station fails unexpectedly, or when conflicting objectives from different stakeholders must be resolved, the system needs more than algorithmic optimization—it needs the ability to recognize the current situation, assemble appropriate objectives, and reason about response strategies\. We introduce Cognitive Intelligence as the third component of the architecture, and the Multi\-Agent System \(MAS\) as the integrating framework\.

Cognitive Intelligence serves as a complementary engine alongside HDC\. While HDC computes accurately within a given scenario using physical models \(the Physical AI engine\), Cognitive Intelligence recognizes which scenario is occurring, assembles the appropriate objective function and constraint set, and reasons about whether the current operating state approaches ODD boundaries \(the Cognitive AI engine\)\. Cognitive Intelligence performs four specific functions: \(i\) scenario classification—recognizing the current operating regime from multivariate sensor data \(e\.g\., distinguishing drought escalation from routine low\-flow conditions\); \(ii\) objective assembly—selecting and weighting the appropriate cost function terms for HDC based on the identified scenario; \(iii\) constraint adaptation—adjusting soft constraint bounds \(e\.g\., tightening environmental flow requirements during ecological stress periods\); and \(iv\) ODD boundary monitoring—estimating proximity to ODD limits and triggering graceful degradation when boundaries are approached\.

A concrete example illustrates the propose\-validate interaction\. Consider a canal system operating under normal delivery \(WSAL\-3\)\. Sensor data indicate declining reservoir inflows over two weeks, while weather forecasts predict continued below\-average precipitation\. Cognitive Intelligence classifies the scenario as 'drought escalation—moderate' and proposes a modified operating configuration: reduce delivery targets to 85% of nominal, tighten water\-level constraints to preserve buffer capacity, and extend the MPC prediction horizon from 12 to 24 steps to improve anticipatory control\. This proposal is formalized as a candidate tuple \{J\_new, g\_new, ODD\_status\}, where J\_new is the modified objective function, g\_new is the tightened constraint set, and ODD\_status indicates whether the proposed configuration remains within the certified ODD\. HDC receives this tuple and performs feasibility validation: does a feasible control trajectory exist under J\_new and g\_new? If yes, the new configuration is adopted\. If no \(e\.g\., the tightened constraints are infeasible given current system state\), HDC rejects the proposal and Cognitive Intelligence must either relax its recommendation or escalate to human oversight\.

The failure mode is explicit: when Cognitive Intelligence operates below a confidence threshold \(calibrated during xIL testing\), the system defaults to the last\-validated HDC configuration—a safe fallback that maintains physics\-based control even when cognitive reasoning is unreliable\. In implementation, Cognitive Intelligence may draw on foundation models for scientific reasoning \(Bommasani et al\., 2021\) and domain\-specific machine learning for hydrological pattern recognition \(Kratzert et al\., 2019\), while the propose\-validate architecture ensures that no data\-driven recommendation bypasses physics\-based safety guarantees\.

The MAS architecture deploys these capabilities through a hierarchy of intelligent agents at three scales\. Edge Agents reside at individual control nodes \(a gate, a pump station, a pressure\-reducing valve\), executing Layer 0–Layer 1 HDC with local sensing and fast response\. Area Agents coordinate groups of edge agents within a hydraulically coupled subsystem \(a canal reach, a reservoir cascade, a district metered area\), running Layer 2 DMPC and managing intra\-area ODD\. Cloud Agents provide system\-wide optimization at Layer 3, integrating Cognitive Intelligence for scenario recognition, inter\-area conflict resolution, and long\-horizon planning\. The critical architectural principle is that each agent is self\-contained: if communication with upper\-level agents is lost, the edge agent continues autonomous operation within its local ODD—an ‘island autonomy’ capability that reflects the slow\-actuator reality \(OS3\) where communication interruptions cannot be allowed to freeze physical actuators mid\-stroke\.

Formally, the MAS architecture can be expressed as: MAS = HDC \+ ODD \+ Cognitive Intelligence\. HDC provides the Physical AI engine \(‘compute accurately’\), ODD defines the safety envelope \(‘operate within certified boundaries’\), and Cognitive Intelligence provides the Cognitive AI engine \(‘reason about situations’\)\. The interaction between these three components is not additive but synergistic: HDC constrains what Cognitive Intelligence may propose, ODD determines when autonomous operation is permitted, and Cognitive Intelligence expands the effective ODD over time by identifying and verifying new scenarios\.

__7\.4  Water Systems Autonomy Levels__

SAE J3016 \(SAE International, 2021\) transformed the automotive industry’s approach to automation by providing a shared taxonomy that clarified what ‘autonomous’ means at each level\. The water sector lacks an equivalent classification\. Building on the preliminary concept in Lei \(2025b\) and drawing on the CHS theory developed in this paper, we propose Water Systems Autonomy Levels \(WSAL\)—a five\-level classification calibrated to the operational singularity constraints of water infrastructure\.

Table 6 defines the five WSAL levels\.

Three features distinguish WSAL from SAE J3016 and reflect the operational singularity of water systems\. First, the ‘bucket principle’: the overall WSAL rating of a water network equals the lowest rating among its constituent subsystems, because a single manually operated gate in an otherwise automated network creates a system\-wide operational bottleneck\. Second, the safety floor is non\-negotiable: regardless of WSAL level, Layer 0 PLC interlocks remain active and no upper\-layer decision—whether from HDC or Cognitive Intelligence—may override them, reflecting OS1 \(failure irreversibility\)\. Third, the WSAL\-2 to WSAL\-3 transition is identified as the critical near\-term challenge: it requires systematic xIL verification to certify ODD boundaries, enabling operators to release manual control within certified conditions\. This transition is the ‘letting go’ moment—analogous to SAE Level 2 to Level 3 in driving—and constitutes the most important practical milestone for the global water sector\.

A cross\-sector assessment reveals that the vast majority of the world’s water infrastructure currently operates at WSAL\-1\. Leading implementations—such as the Shaoping cascade hydropower station’s MPC\-based real\-time optimization \(Ye et al\., 2023\) and the Jiaodong inter\-basin water transfer project’s multi\-timescale planning\-control integration \(Lei et al\., 2025b\)—have achieved WSAL\-2 for specific subsystems under typical operating scenarios\. No operational water system has yet reached WSAL\-3, making the WSAL\-2→3 transition the frontier of both research and engineering practice\.
